target_claim: Running Dijkstra's algorithm (re-insertion variant) from s on the explicitly defined layered DAG Gn performs Omega(2^n) successful Relax operations.
source_quote:
Theorem 1. When Dijkstra’s algorithm processes Gn starting from source s, it performs
Ω(2n) successful Relax operations.
test_sketch: Implement Gn exactly as defined (lines 0017-0035: source s; vertices v_{i,b} for 1<=i<=n-1, b in {0,1}; sink t; edges s->v_{1,b} weight 0, v_{i,0}->v_{i+1,b} weight +2^i, v_{i,1}->v_{i+1,b} weight -2^i+1, v_{n-1,b}->t weight 0) and run Dijkstra with lazy re-insertion on distance decrease (line 0097), counting successful Relax operations (d[v] actually updated) via an instrumented counter. Run for n = 4..12 and compare the counter against c*2^n. Expected refutation: counts grow linearly (~2 per vertex, O(n)), because the most-negative all-ones path is extracted FIRST by the priority queue (v_{1,1} at key 0 pushes level-2 entries at key -1, which pop before v_{1,0} at key 0, and so on down), so each vertex's distance is set to its final value on its first '1'-parent relaxation and never decreases again; no cascading re-relaxations occur. Cross-check with a brute-force enumeration of all 2^{n-1} path weights confirming the all-ones path is the minimum discovered immediately. The construction has the sign structure backwards for an exponential counterexample (which requires the shortest path to be discovered last), so the Omega(2^n) operation-count claim fails measurably at every tested n.
